title: The King of Tyre Who Said, I Am a God
summary: God confronts the ruler of Tyre, whose wealth and wisdom have made him claim to be a god; foreigners will bring him down to death, and he will prove to be only a man. A lament then pictures the king as a glorious figure in Eden, the garden of God, adorned with precious stones and placed on God's holy mountain, until pride and violent trade corrupted him and he was cast out. Short oracles against Sidon and a promise of Israel's secure return close the chapter.
story: This chapter completes the three-chapter oracle against Tyre. Chapter 26 announced the city's fall, chapter 27 lamented it as a sunken ship, and chapter 28 goes to the heart of the matter: the pride of Tyre's ruler, which is the pride of the city itself. After a brief word against Sidon, Tyre's older sister city, the chapter turns for a moment to Israel. Verses 24 to 26 promise that when God has judged the neighbors who despised his people, he will gather Israel from the nations and let them live securely in their land. That promise anticipates the restoration chapters of the book (34 to 37) and marks the midpoint of the oracles against the nations, before the long series against Egypt begins in chapter 29.
historical:
The chapter does not name the king. According to Josephus, who cites Phoenician records, the king of Tyre during Nebuchadnezzar's long siege was Ithobaal, sometimes called Ethbaal III. Whoever held the throne, the oracle addresses the office and what it had come to represent: a ruler whose city had grown immensely rich through trade and who stood, in his own eyes, beyond the reach of any power. Kings in the ancient Near East often claimed a special closeness to the gods, and some were honored as divine or semi-divine.

Sidon, about twenty miles north of Tyre, was the older of the two great Phoenician cities, and the name Sidonians was sometimes used for Phoenicians generally. Sidon had been part of the western coalition against Babylon (Jeremiah 27:3). Israel's history with Sidon was long and troubled: Jezebel, the queen who promoted Baal worship in Israel, was the daughter of Ethbaal, king of the Sidonians (1 Kings 16:31).
cultural:
Verse 3 compares the king's wisdom to Daniel's. The spelling in the Hebrew is Dan'el, and interpreters differ over whether this is the Daniel of the book of Daniel, a younger contemporary of Ezekiel in Babylon, or an ancient figure known for wisdom and righteousness, since a just king named Danel appears in texts from Ugarit, a Canaanite city whose tablets date to the late second millennium BC. Ezekiel also names Daniel with Noah and Job as righteous men (14:14, 20).

The lament in verses 12 to 19 draws on imagery a priest like Ezekiel knew well. Eden, the garden of God, is the first sanctuary in Scripture. The cherubim were the guardian creatures who barred the way to the tree of life (Genesis 3:24) and whose images covered the ark in the tabernacle (Exodus 25:18-22). The mountain of God and the fiery stones suggest God's dwelling place. The precious stones in verse 13 are all found among the twelve stones on the high priest's breastpiece (Exodus 28:17-20), and the Greek translation of Ezekiel lists all twelve. The king is pictured in the dress of a priest-king in God's own sanctuary, which makes his fall a desecration.
literary: The chapter has four units. Verses 1 to 10 are a judgment oracle in the standard because and therefore form, built on the contrast between I am a god and you are a man. Verses 11 to 19 are a lament (qinah) that tells the king's story as a fall from glory: created, adorned, placed on God's mountain, blameless until wickedness was found in him, then expelled and burned to ashes. Its Hebrew is difficult in places, especially verses 14 and 16, which can be read either as calling the king himself the guardian cherub (as the BSB does) or as saying he was placed with a cherub who later drove him out; the Greek translation takes the second view. Verses 20 to 23 are a brief oracle against Sidon, and verses 24 to 26 turn to Israel's future. The repeated they will know that I am the LORD ties the whole together.

outline.t: The ruler of Tyre claims to be a god
Brought down: a man and not a god
Lament: the king in Eden, perfect until wickedness was found
Cast from the mountain of God and consumed

doctrines.note: The chapter traces sin to its root in pride: a heart that claims the place of God. Wealth and wisdom were gifts, but the king used them to make himself the center, and trade became violence (verse 16).

God's answer to the king is simple: you are a man, and not a god (verse 2). Human dignity is real, but it is creaturely. The fall pictured in verses 12 to 19 echoes the first human beings' reaching to be like God.
Verses 25 and 26 promise that God will gather his scattered people and let them live securely, build houses, and plant vineyards. Judgment on the proud is paired with care for the humbled.

words.note: El, god. The king says, I am a god, using the most basic Semitic word for deity, which was also the name of the high god in Canaanite religion. The chapter answers with the word for a human being, adam: you are a man.

Keruv, cherub, one of the winged guardian beings associated with God's throne and sanctuary. They guarded Eden after the expulsion (Genesis 3:24) and overshadowed the ark. Whether the king is called a cherub or placed alongside one depends on how the Hebrew of verse 14 is read.

Chokhmah, wisdom, including practical skill. The king's wisdom was real and made him rich (verse 4), but he corrupted it because of his splendor (verse 17). In the Bible wisdom rightly used begins with the fear of the LORD.

Gavah, to be high or lifted up, and so to be proud. It describes the king's heart in verses 2, 5, and 17. The imagery of height runs through the chapter: the proud king on the mountain of God is cast down to the earth.

christ: The king of Tyre grasped at divinity and was brought down. The New Testament describes Christ as the opposite: though he was in the form of God, he did not consider equality with God something to be grasped, but emptied himself and took the form of a servant (Philippians 2:6-8). Where the king corrupted his wisdom, Christ is called the wisdom of God (1 Corinthians 1:24). And if the lament's Eden imagery recalls Adam, the human being placed in God's garden who reached for what was not his, the New Testament presents Jesus as the last Adam who obeyed where the first failed (Romans 5:19; 1 Corinthians 15:45). Jesus also visited the region of Tyre and Sidon, where a Gentile woman's faith met his mercy (Mark 7:24-30), a quiet sign that the nations under judgment in Ezekiel were not outside God's reach. These are connections drawn by later writers, not predictions in the chapter itself.

hard.q: Is the lament in verses 12 to 19 about Satan's fall?
hard.a:
The text's own horizon comes first. The oracle is addressed to the king of Tyre (verse 12), and the charges against him are the charges of chapters 26 and 27: pride, dishonest trade, and violence (verses 16 and 18). The Eden imagery fits a human figure: the first human beings were placed in the garden, created good, and expelled when they reached for what belonged to God. Many interpreters therefore read the lament as describing the king in the language of the first human fall, perhaps also drawing on older traditions about a primal figure in the garden of God, to say that his pride repeats Adam's and deserves the same exile. Others read the lament as the king's self-image turned against him: he saw himself as a divine being in paradise, and God takes up that picture to show how far he will fall.

From early in the church's history, however, many Christians read the passage as a picture of Satan's fall. Writers such as Tertullian and Origen applied it to the devil, often alongside Isaiah 14:12-15, and the reading has remained common in popular Christian teaching and in some evangelical scholarship. Its defenders argue that the language of being in Eden, a guardian cherub, and blameless from the day of creation goes beyond any human king, and that the prophet looks through the earthly ruler to the spiritual power behind his pride, much as the New Testament speaks of spiritual forces behind earthly rulers (Ephesians 6:12). Those who hesitate note that the New Testament never cites this passage in connection with Satan, that the Hebrew of the cherub verses is uncertain, and that the passage's point is aimed at human arrogance. Both readings agree on the lesson: pride that grasps at God's place ends in ruin.

questions: The king's pride grew out of real gifts, wisdom and skill in trade. How can good gifts become the very things that make us proud?
God's answer to the king is, you are a man and not a god. What would it look like to accept your limits as a creature gladly rather than resentfully?
Verses 25 and 26 promise security to a scattered people. Where do you long for that kind of security, and where are you seeking it?
